title: Some Trust in Chariots: A Prayer for the King
summary: The people pray for their king on the day of trouble, asking the LORD to answer him, send help from Zion, accept his offerings, and grant his plans. A single voice then declares confidence that the LORD saves his anointed. The psalm sets those who trust in chariots and horses against those who trust in the name of the LORD, and ends with a plea for God to save the king.
story: Psalm 20 is a short royal psalm that pairs naturally with Psalm 21. Here the people pray for the king before a battle; in Psalm 21 they give thanks after the victory. Coming after the royal thanksgiving of Psalm 18 and the praise of God's law in Psalm 19, it shows the king not as a self-made warrior but as a man carried by the prayers of his people and dependent on God's name. It reflects the covenant with David in 2 Samuel 7, in which God promised to be a father to David's line, and it keeps in view the old warning of Deuteronomy 17:16 that Israel's king must not multiply horses for himself.
historical:
The heading reads For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. Traditional readers take it as written by David for use in the temple worship he organized; many modern scholars read of David as marking a royal or Davidic collection and see the psalm as a liturgy used for kings of David's line whenever they went out to war. The psalm itself refers to Zion and the sanctuary, which suggests a setting in Jerusalem after the ark was brought there, and to burnt offerings made before battle, a practice mentioned in 1 Samuel 13:9-12, where Saul offers one before fighting the Philistines.

The psalm has a remarkable later echo. An Aramaic text written in Egyptian Demotic script, known as Papyrus Amherst 63 and usually dated to around the fourth century BC, contains a prayer closely resembling the opening verses of Psalm 20, but addressed to other gods, including the Egyptian god Horus. Scholars debate how the two are related. Some think the papyrus adapts a hymn that came from Israel, others that both draw on a shared tradition of royal prayer. Either way, the parallel shows how widely such language circulated, and how distinctive Israel's version is in giving the whole trust to the LORD alone.
cultural:
Chariots were the most advanced military technology of the ancient Near East, used by Egypt, the Canaanite city-states, and Assyria. A chariot force was expensive and required horses, trained drivers, and flat ground, and a nation's power was often counted in them. Israel in the hill country had few chariots for much of its history, and its story began with Pharaoh's chariots sunk in the sea (Exodus 15:4). Solomon later built up large chariot forces (1 Kings 10:26), exactly the kind of power the prophets warned against trusting (Isaiah 31:1).

Banners in verse 5 were raised in battle as rallying points and in victory as signs of triumph. The name of God, mentioned three times in this short psalm, stood in Israel's thinking for God's revealed character and presence; to trust in the name was to rely on who God had shown himself to be. Before battle, kings consulted God and offered sacrifice, and the people's prayer that God would remember the king's offerings reflects that practice.
literary: The psalm is a liturgy with more than one voice. Verses 1 to 5 are the congregation's prayer for the king, a string of wishes each beginning may, addressed to the king in the second person. Verse 6 shifts suddenly to a single speaker (Now I know), perhaps a priest or prophet who declares that the prayer has been heard, or perhaps the king himself. Verses 7 and 8 are a sharp contrast in parallel lines: they trust chariots, we trust the name; they collapse and fall, we rise and stand. Verse 9 returns to the community's petition. The word answer frames the whole psalm, opening in verse 1 and closing in verse 9.

outline.t: The people's prayer for the king on the day of trouble
Now I know: the LORD saves his anointed
Chariots and horses, or the name of the LORD

doctrines.note: Verse 7 sets trust in the name of the LORD against trust in military power. Faith here is not an escape from action (the king still goes to battle) but a refusal to locate security in what human strength can buy.
The whole community prays for its leader, and one voice announces the answer. The psalm teaches intercession for those who carry responsibility, and confidence that God hears.
The king is God's anointed, and his victory comes from God's right hand. Human rule in Israel was meant to depend on and display God's rule, not replace it.

words.note: Shem, name. In the Bible a name often carries a person's identity and reputation. God's name stands for his revealed character and his presence with his people (Exodus 34:5-7). The psalm uses it three times, and verse 7 makes it the object of trust: not a magic word, but the God who had made himself known.

Mashiach, anointed. Israel's kings were anointed with oil when installed, and the word became a title for the king God had chosen. From it comes the English word Messiah, and through the Greek translation, Christ. In verse 6 it is the reigning king of David's line.

Rekev, chariot or chariotry. The word can mean a single vehicle or a whole chariot force. In Israel's memory it recalled Pharaoh's army at the sea, and in the prophets it became a symbol of misplaced trust in military power.

Tsiyyon, Zion. Originally the fortified hill David captured from the Jebusites (2 Samuel 5:7), the name came to stand for Jerusalem and especially the temple mount, the place where God had chosen to make his name dwell. Help comes from Zion because God's presence is there.

christ: Psalm 20 is a prayer for the anointed king, and the New Testament proclaims Jesus as the anointed King of David's line. The psalm's pattern (the king facing the day of trouble, the people praying, and God answering from heaven with the saving power of his right hand) finds its fullest shape in the cross and resurrection, where God raised his anointed and seated him at his right hand (Acts 2:32-36). The New Testament doesn't quote this psalm, so the link is thematic. It also clarifies the kind of king Jesus is: he refused the sword and the chariot, entered Jerusalem on a donkey (Matthew 21:5), and trusted his Father's name to the end. The contrast of verse 7 runs through his whole ministry.
questions: What are the chariots and horses of your own life, the resources you instinctively trust when trouble comes?
The people pray for their king before battle. Who are the leaders you could pray for in this way, and what would you ask for them?
In verse 6 a voice says, “Now I know.” What helps you move from praying about something to trusting that God has heard?
